title: Old Python for Windows Control Panel entries still exist after upgrades
author: jimdunn

text:
The traditional python.org Windows installer uses a WiX Burn bootstrapper per major.minor.micro release. If %LocalAppData%\Package Cache is cleaned up (by Disk Cleanup, Storage Sense, or a third-party cleaner) before an in-place upgrade runs, the new installer upgrades the MSI payloads in your Python directory but cannot execute the cached old bootstrapper .exe to unregister the prior version’s ARP entry.
That leaves orphaned Uninstall keys under HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\{GUID} (or HKLM for all-users installs). You can inspect and remove the stale entries cleanly in PowerShell without redownloading every old .exe:
Get-ItemProperty HKCU:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\* |
  Where-Object { $_.DisplayName -like "Python 3.*" } |
  Select-Object DisplayName, DisplayVersion, PSChildName

Removing the specific PSChildName registry key for the superseded point releases clears them from appwiz.cpl immediately.
author: jaharoni

text: The Package Cache explanation fits what I’ve seen — those orphaned ARP entries are just leftover Uninstall keys, not a broken install. One caution on the PowerShell approach: filter on DisplayName and verify the InstallLocation or Publisher before deleting, since other Python distributions can share similar names. Also worth noting all-users installs need an elevated session to touch the HKLM keys, and exporting each key first makes rollback easy if you remove the wrong one. Does removing just the key affect anything the MSI still references, or is it purely cosmetic?
